stops.name: Shigatse, the Master's letter to the family at Odessa
stops.campa: In Odessa the aunt Nadyezhda, sick with two years' silence and fearing Helena dead, opens a letter that no post carried and no hand delivered. It simply appears. Written in French in a fine unknown script and signed with a Rajput name, it bids the family be at peace: their beloved is safe, far away in a retreat beyond reach, and shall be restored to them. Master Koot Hoomi has spoken across half the earth to comfort her people. The letter becomes a family relic and the first of the phenomena the world will later fight over. The Brotherhood, it says plainly, is real.
stops.quote: The noble relations of Mad. H. Blavatsky have no cause whatever for grief. Their daughter and niece has not left this world at all.
stops.quote_source: The Koot Hoomi letter to Nadyezhda Fadeyev, 1870 (Incidents in the Life of Madame Blavatsky)

stops.name: Off Spetsai, the wreck of the Eumonia
stops.campa: Sailing from Piraeus toward Egypt aboard the steamer Eumonia, she is caught in disaster when the ship's powder or fireworks cargo blows apart off the island of Spetsai. The vessel is torn open and most aboard are drowned or burned; she is flung into the sea and comes ashore with nothing: no money, no luggage, only her life. Passed again through fire and water and unscathed, as the font foretold, she reaches Alexandria a penniless survivor. The sea has stripped her to begin again, and she goes up to Cairo to raise the dead of a different kind.

stops.name: Cairo, the Société Spirite founders in scandal
stops.campa: In Cairo she founds a Société Spirite to test the mediums and sift the true from the false in the fashionable spirit-craze. It collapses inside a fortnight: the hired mediums drink, cheat, and produce their marvels with gauze and wire; a madman breaks in upon a séance; the money vanishes. Here too she first meets Emma Cutting, the future Madame Coulomb, who lends her cash and will one day become her destroyer. She writes home in disgust that the spooks of the séance-room are no spirits at all but the cast-off skins of the dead. She has learned the fraud from the inside.
stops.quote: Their spirits are no spirits but spooks — rags, the cast off second skins of their personalities that the dead shed in the astral light as serpents shed theirs on earth.
stops.quote_source: H. P. Blavatsky, letter of 1872 (from Cairo)

stops.name: New York, landing penniless at the Master's order
stops.campa: The order comes from the Master while she is in Paris: go to America. On the seventh of July she steps off the ship at New York with almost nothing in her purse, and when she sees a poor woman in worse straits she gives away her last coin. For a season the future oracle of the age lives in a tenement and sews cravats and makes artificial flowers for her bread. She waits, as she has learned to wait, knowing the summons will make sense in its own time. The New World that will make her famous first makes her a seamstress.

stops.name: Chittenden, Vermont: the meeting with Olcott at the Eddy farm
stops.campa: At the Eddy brothers' haunted farmstead in Vermont, where spirit-forms are said to walk nightly out of a cabinet, she comes to see the phenomena, and to be seen. Henry Steel Olcott, a Civil-War colonel turned investigating journalist, notices the Russian in the red Garibaldi shirt across the room, offers her a light for her cigarette, and the great collaboration of both their lives ignites over a match. Within days the phenomena at the farm grow strange and vivid in her presence. The soldier of Rome has found her second soldier; together they will found a Society and remake the spiritual map of the West.

stops.name: New York, the founding of the Theosophical Society
stops.campa: In her rooms at Irving Place, after George Felt's lecture on the lost canon of proportion in the Egyptian temples, the talk turns to founding a body to study the hidden side of nature and the powers latent in man. Olcott passes a note proposing a society; Judge seconds it; Helena assents. Within days the name is chosen, Theosophical, meaning the divine wisdom, and on the seventeenth of November it is launched to the public with Olcott as President and Blavatsky its living oracle. From a New York parlour a movement is born that will carry the word of the Masters around the earth.

stops.name: The Lamasery: Isis Unveiled written under dictation
stops.campa: In the cluttered flat on Forty-Seventh Street they call the Lamasery, hung with Eastern silks, a stuffed baboon in a wing-collar clutching lecture notes in mockery of Darwin, where she writes Isis Unveiled through the nights. She quotes books she has never opened and cannot have; passages appear before her in the air and she copies them down; the Master, she says, dictates and her hand obeys. Twelve hundred pages come forth, and a thousand copies sell in ten days. Her first great work declares one primeval wisdom-religion beneath all faiths, and the veil of the goddess is lifted for the modern world.
stops.quote: The work now submitted to public judgment is the fruit of a somewhat intimate acquaintance with Eastern adepts and study of their science.
stops.quote_source: H. P. Blavatsky, Isis Unveiled (1877), preface

stops.name: Bombay, the Founders arrive in the land of the Masters
stops.campa: The Master's order to leave for India comes, and the two Founders sail. On the sixteenth of February Blavatsky and Olcott step ashore at Bombay and kiss the ground of the sacred land, the first Western spiritual teachers to come to India not to convert her but to sit at her feet. They take a house on Girgaum Back Road, hire the boy Babula, and open the true headquarters of the movement in the country of its origin. Hindus and Parsis flock to the strange Russian who honours their scriptures above the missionaries' Bible. The tide of Theosophy turns eastward, homeward, at last.

stops.name: Allahabad and the meeting of Sinnett and Hume
stops.campa: At Allahabad she wins the two Englishmen who will make the Masters famous and infamous. A. P. Sinnett, editor of the Pioneer, and A. O. Hume of the Indian Civil Service open their houses and their minds to her, hungry for proof of the Brotherhood. Through her they begin to correspond with Morya and Koot Hoomi themselves, letters passing by no earthly post. Out of this contact will come Sinnett's Occult World and Esoteric Buddhism, and the whole archive of Mahatma letters. She has handed the hidden Masters two English pens; the phenomena are about to go to press.

stops.name: Kandy, Ceylon: taking the Buddhist pansil
stops.campa: In Ceylon, before the monks and a great crowd, Blavatsky and Olcott kneel and take pansil, the five precepts, and become, formally and publicly, Buddhists, the first Westerners of note to do so on Buddhist soil. The island rejoices; the Sinhalese see in these two white foreigners defenders sent to raise their faith against the missionaries. Olcott will go on to design the Buddhist flag and write the catechism; Blavatsky lends the movement her fame. The wanderer who studied at Tashilhunpo now bows to the Dharma in the open, and the East claims her as its own.

stops.name: Simla, the phenomena of the brooch and the cup
stops.campa: In the hill-station of Simla she makes the wonders that will ring round the Empire. At a picnic where a seventh guest lacks a cup, she holds a silent word with a Brother, points into the ground, and a china cup and saucer are dug from the untouched earth. A brooch that Mrs. Sinnett left at home is found sewn inside a cushion no one has opened. A note torn and vanished from her hand reappears among the branches of a tree, signed in Tibetan characters. Sinnett prints it all in The Occult World, and the astonished West sends its investigators east to catch her out.

stops.name: Sikkim, the Master seen in the mountains
stops.campa: Dying of a kidney disease that has nearly stopped her heart, she is called north to the border of Sikkim and there, on the edge of the forbidden land, she meets Master Morya in his own body, not a vision but the man, warm and living, who heals her with a look and gives her the strength to go on. She comes back down transfigured, the illness lifted, witnesses swearing she left a wreck and returned whole. The Brotherhood is not a memory of Tibet but a present power that reaches down out of the snows to keep its instrument alive for the work still unwritten.
